newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Jan 23.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Jan 23.

text.p: The Children, Young Persons and Families Service has told the government it desperately needs money to cope with a tide of child abuse, neglect and crime. Briefing papers to the government say the Social Welfare Department and the community believe the service has been underfunded for years. The service's budget for the 1996-97 financial year was almost $160 million, including an $11 million increase on the year before. However, the department says the service needs an extra $30 million a year. Page 1.

The Social Welfare Department has suggested handing over the money spent on benefits to private sector organisations such as Maori tribes to administer. This is one option for changes to the benefit system it says are necessary. The department used its briefing papers to tell Social Welfare Minister Roger Sowry he will have to look at fundamental changes to benefits if the government wants to reduce welfare dependency significantly. Page 2.

Prime Minister Jim Bolger will become the first New Zealand prime minister to set foot at the South Pole. He is to fly with a small party from Scott Base to the pole to spend time at the United States-run scientific establishment there. Mr Bolger and his wife Joan are on a four-day visit to Antarctica to commemorate the 40th anniversary of the establishment of a permanent New Zealand presence on Antarctica, at Scott Base. They are part of a 14-member party that includes Sir Edmund Hilary. Page 2.

A secret beneficial shareholding by Fay Richwhite and Brierley Investments in Laverton Securities could have been one of the scenarios behind a mystery payment of nearly $2 million to the two companies, the Cook Islands tax commission of inquiry in Auckland was told on Wednesday. The payment, known as the "Laverton adjustment" was made to Fay Richwhite and Brierley in 1990 and each company received $808,500. The commission had earlier heard that though the Laverton adjustment had arisen several times during the long inquiry into the Cook Islands tax haven and the participation of New Zealand companies in tax credits, no one had been able to explain it. Page 2.

Transporting nuclear waste through the Pacific and possibly the Tasman Sea did increase the risk to people in the region, the Foreign Affairs and Trade Ministry said on Wednesday. Officials from the ministry, Maritime Safety Authority, Defence, and the Prime Minister and Cabinet Department spent two and a half hours at a briefing by representatives from the British transporter and the French and Japanese nuclear power companies on Wednesday afternoon. Page 2.

Police Minister Jack Elder and Labour justice spokesman Phil Goff would meet today to discuss plans to put dangerous Asian Triad gangs out of business in New Zealand, Goff said on Wednesday. Goff, recently returned from Hong Kong where he met police and officials to discuss triads, said he welcomed a multi-agency task-force to pressure Triad connections in New Zealand and to increase the costs and risks of extending their operations here. Page 2.

Stopping New Zealand's unique animals and plants from becoming extinct remains the highest priority for the Conservation Department, chief executive Bill Mansfield says. In the department's briefing paper to the incoming government, he says that turning around the decline in New Zealand's bio-diversity is the biggest challenge facing the department. Page 2.

The Agriculture Ministry's decision to add a round of public consultation over introduction of the rabbit calicivirus has angered farmers but heartened opponents. The ministry said that the 800 submitters and the group applying to import the virus would have a chance to comment on a review of their submissions by a ministry-appointed group of experts and government departments. Page 7.

The government was wise to have opted against passing a law to abolish the final right of appeal to the Privy Council in London, the New Zealand Law Society said on Wednesday. Society president Austin Forbes, QC, said opposition to such a move was widespread from Parliament and groups including Maori, business people and the legal profession. Justice Minister Doug Graham said that though he still believed the time had come to drop the avenue of last resort to the Privy Council, it was clear that too few MPs were prepared to support the measure. Richina Pacific, formerly the Mainzeal Group, has entered into a conditional contract to sell its extensive car-park operations. A confidentiality agreement surrounds the deal, but it is understood that Wilson Parking, a multi-national parking operations company with New Zealand headquarters in Wellington, is the buyer. Richina's Mainzeal Parking operates about 20 car parks with a capacity of more than 8000 vehicles in Wellington, Auckland and Hamilton. Page 13.

IBM New Zealand lost $9 million on almost flat revenues in 1995 in a performance managing director Gowan Pickering blamed on the economy. He said IBM's result for the year ending December 31 was adversely affected by second-half economic conditions that caused a downturn in equipment expenditure, and by fierce competition and margin pressure. IBM, New Zealand's biggest computer company, reported revenues of $282 million, 2.1 percent up on last year's record $276 million, but well below expected results of more than $300 million. Page 13.

New interest rates for overpaid and underpaid tax would be introduced starting next month, Revenue Minister Bill Birch said this week. He said from February 7 the interest rate on overpayments of provisional tax would be 7.1 percent a year, down from 8.2 percent, and the rate for underpayments would be 13.9 percent, up from 13.8 percent. Page 13.

High fuel costs and the strong dollar have analysts set to lower their forecasts for Air New Zealand's June 1997 profit. Latest indications suggest that the carrier's earnings will be about $180 million -- assuming jet fuel prices fall and the doller softens. Expectations for this year started at about $200 million after a 13 percent slump in June 1996-year earnings to $225 million was announced last September. In December, that figure was lowered to a market average of $190 million. Page 13.

Electricity Corporation of New Zealand said on Wednesday it would invest $50 million in upgrading the Waitaki hydro power scheme. Generation general manager Kieran Devine said an increase of at least one percent efficiency from the power scheme was expected to result from this project, equal to an increase in output of 125 gigawatt hours, enough to meet the domestic consumption of 16,000 households. Page 13.

Otter Gold reported on Wednesday an increase in overall gold output and ore reserves for the three months to December, compared with the preceding three months. Gold production at its Martha Mine joint venture, in which it has a 33 percent interest, was up 10 percent to 21,301 ounces, from 19,442 for the previous period. The increase was largely due to the higher grade of ore mined, the company said. Page 13.
